messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Exponential Prior for GMRF parameters
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Exponential Prior for GMRF parameters
messages.body_plain:
These considerations are on the linear predictor level, not on the hyper-parameter level. For the types of details you are intreested in, the paper by Simpson et al is where to go:
https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ss/1491465621

Haakon

On Sat, 14 Sep 2019 at 13:22, 'Herbert Meier' via R-inla discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Thanks so much for your reply!
>
> I have two follow-up question: When you say
> > The idea presented here is that the amount of "randomness" (or variation) you want to include in the spatial term should have the same penalty no matter how much you have "already included".
> does the "already included" refer to all (r,σ_u,σ_e) whose prior I assume to be exponential? Or what is explicitly meant by that (what are those other sources that could lead to variation in the spatial model)?
>
> Is it possible to formalize that rationale? Given the above mentioned definition of  the memory-less property, what would X constitute?
>
>

messages.subject_clean: Problem generating samples using inla.posterior.sample()
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've recently updated to the most recent version of INLA (19.09.03) and I appear to have a problem generating samples using the  inla.posterior.sample() function.

Previously, when I generated samples I would get the samples of the latent field indexed by what was in the INLA object for example:

> row.names(samp[[1]]$latent)[grep('Region1:',row.names(samp[[1]]$latent))]
  [1] "Region1:Asia Pacific, High Income"    "Region1:Asia, Central"                "Region1:Asia, East"                   "Region1:Asia, South"                  "Region1:Asia, Southeast"
  [6] "Region1:Australasia"                  "Region1:Caribbean"                    "Region1:Europe, Central"              "Region1:Europe, Eastern"              "Region1:Europe, Western"
 [11] "Region1:Latin America, Andean"        "Region1:Latin America, Central"       "Region1:Latin America, Southern"      "Region1:Latin America, Tropical"      "Region1:North Africa / Middle East"
 [16] "Region1:North America, High Income"   "Region1:Oceania"                      "Region1:Sub-Saharan Africa, East"     "Region1:Sub-Saharan Africa, Southern" "Region1:Sub-Saharan Africa, West"
 [21] "Region1:Unknown"                      "Region1:1"                            "Region1:2"                            "Region1:3"                            "Region1:4"
 [26] "Region1:5"                            "Region1:6"                            "Region1:7"                            "Region1:8"                            "Region1:9"
 [31] "Region1:10"                           "Region1:11"                           "Region1:12"                           "Region1:13"                           "Region1:14"

 [41] "Region1:20"                           "Region1:21"                           "Region1:1"                            "Region1:2"                            "Region1:3"

But in the new version, I seem to lose this indexing for example:

> row.names(samp[[1]]$latent)[grep('Region1:',row.names(samp[[1]]$latent))]
  [1] "Region1:1"   "Region1:2"   "Region1:3"   "Region1:4"   "Region1:5"   "Region1:6"   "Region1:7"   "Region1:8"   "Region1:9"   "Region1:10"  "Region1:11"  "Region1:12"  "Region1:13"  "Region1:14"  "Region1:15"

 [31] "Region1:31"  "Region1:32"  "Region1:33"  "Region1:34"  "Region1:35"  "Region1:36"  "Region1:37"  "Region1:38"  "Region1:39"  "Region1:40"  "Region1:41"  "Region1:42"  "Region1:43"  "Region1:44"  "Region1:45"
 [46] "Region1:46"  "Region1:47"  "Region1:48"  "Region1:49"  "Region1:50"  "Region1:51"  "Region1:52"  "Region1:53"  "Region1:54"  "Region1:55"  "Region1:56"  "Region1:57"  "Region1:58"  "Region1:59"  "Region1:60"

so my code can't match the samples with the corresponding Regions that I'm interested in.

Is there an reason why this is happening? Or is there an obvious fix?

Thanks in advance
Matt

messages.subject: prediction questions: fitted values on the link function and selecting values for prediction
messages.subject_clean: prediction questions: fitted values on the link function and selecting values for prediction
messages.body_plain:
I have two questions.

1.  When prediction is desired on additional values that are not part of the INLA model, one method is to append those additional rows to the original data set, set the outcome variable to `NA`, feed the combined new dataset to INLA, and alert INLA that it needs to predict those NA values.  When a link function is involved, `control.predictor=list(link=1)' advises INLA that it needs to provide fitted values for all submitted rows on the scale of the original response variable.

At times, though, it is useful to have posterior predictions that are still on the scale of the link function.  Something along the lines of `posterer_linpred` from the rstanarm package.  Is there a way to generate posterior predictions still on the scale of the link function using some sort of other indicator?

I suppose I could also just sample from the distributions of the fitted values on the original scale and convert them back to the link, but that would be less efficient and it is unclear if doing so could impact accuracy.

2.  At times, practitioners care ONLY about the new values for prediction purposes, and not at all about fitted values on the training data used by the model.  Is the time required to generate predictions at all impacted by the number of rows that need to be predicted?  If so, perhaps there is or could be a flag to predict *only* rows with NA values? If this would save substantial prediction time for larger models, it could be useful.  If it makes no difference, then of course there is no point.  But I wanted to ask.

Thanks much,
Jonathan

I have multiple time-series and I would like to use rw1 to obtain a single average smoothed time-series. The problems are (1) missing data so for some time-series we do not have the first few years of data and (2) the mean values of each time-series are rather different, but I am not interested in the differences in means, only in the changes of values among years.

I planned to fit the model
inla1 <- inla(ts ~ 1 + f(dataset,model="iid") + f(year,model="rw1"),data=mydata)
but it is giving unexpected results as seen in the following dummy dataset.

#5 timeseries with 6 years - all of which are increasing in value over time
ts1 <- c(100,120,125,130,140,145)
ts2 <- c(90,110,115,120,125,125)
ts3 <- c(NA,NA,NA,40,45,50)#lower values but still increasing + missing data in early years
ts4 <- c(NA,NA,NA,30,35,40)#lower values but still increasing + missing data in early years
ts5 <- c(NA,NA,NA,NA,25,35)#lower values but still increasing + missing data in early years

#combine into data frame
ts <- c(ts1,ts2,ts3,ts4,ts5)
year <-rep (c(1,2,3,4,5,6),5)
dataset <- rep(1:5,each=6)
df <- data.frame(year,ts,dataset)

library(INLA)
inla1 <- inla(ts ~ 1 + f(dataset,model="iid") + f(year,model="rw1"),
              control.predictor = list(link = 1),data=df)
inla1$summary.random$year$mean
1.126016e-05  1.024198e-05  5.570443e-06 -3.413189e-06 -1.048947e-05 -1.320624e-05

In this model the random walk is becoming more negative even though all separate ts are increasing. I guess that is because the time series with lower mean values have missing data in the first few years.

The dataset random intercept does not seem to be accounting for the differences in mean values as I thought (?). I would appreciate advice on where I am going wrong.

messages.body_plain:
Hi & thanks for your email.

there are several issues here.

different mean ->  us a factor
different time series -> use replicate
common 'trend' -> model the trend explicitely
missing values -> use 'values'

H

##length of each time series
n = 50
## number of time series
nt = 10
## the time points you want to define the time series.
## defining them explictely, you do not need
## to have them present in the first index.
values = 1:n

## data
y = c()
## the different means in each time-series
mu.value = rnorm(nt)
## a common trend
trend = sin(0.3 * 1:n)
for(i in 1:nt) {
    y = c(y,  trend +
              mu.value[i] +
              c(scale(arima.sim(n, model = list(ar = 0.95)))))
}

r = inla(y ~ -1 +
             mu +
             f(idx, model = "rw2", scale.model=TRUE, values = values) +
             f(idx2,  model = "ar1", replicate = r, values = values),
         data = data.frame(mu = as.factor(rep(1:nt, each = n)),
                           y = y,
                           idx = rep(1:n, nt),
                           idx2 = rep(1:n, nt),
                           r = rep(1:nt, each = n)))

plot(r)

messages.subject: Barrier model marginal variances
messages.subject_clean: Barrier model marginal variances
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am using the barrier model, and have a question about extracting the variance of the spatial effect.

In the classical SPDE model, we can simply use "inla.spde2.result", but because of how barrier model is defined (generic) this doesn't work.

So I assumed that the way to go is to take Theta1, transform Theta1 = log(sigma), and use that sigma to get the variance, via the inla.tmarginal(function(x) exp(x), Theta1).

But when I tried to use the same procedure on the non-barrier SPDE model (just to validate if this works), the result by using theta1 resulted with the different value that the "inla.spde2.result".

In short, could you please confirm, what would be the proper way for obtaining marginal variances for the spatial effect in the barrier model, so that the resulting variance would be comparable to the result of the inla.spde2.result?

Thanks and regards,
Ivan Pocrnic

The Roslin Institute
The University of Edinburgh

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I don’t have a good answer for the barrier model itself, but be aware that the
parameterisation for the regular spde2.matern models is user defined, and that
the default parameterisation is _not_ log(sigma); this is the reason I wrote the spde.result function, to have a unified way to access the humanly interpretable
properties of the estimated model. In principle, the barrier models could/should
have similar code written and linked in to the generic system.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Finn and Haakon,

Thank you both for the clear, precise and very fast replies! I really appreciate it.

First of all, thanks for confirming the correct way to obtain Var for the barrier model.

Regarding the non-barrier model, I was testing before only by “inla.spde2.matern”, and the results were not comparable as I already mentioned in my first post. On the other hand, when I tried “inla.spde2.pcmatern” after your comment, and being careful for the swapped ordering now, I got exactly the same values both by using “inla.spde2.result” and by using “inla.tmarginal(function(x) exp(x), …)”.

I have to admit that this would be hard to figure out without your tips, as some of the internal parameterizations are cryptic. For example summary() of model run by “inla.spde2.matern” is reporting Theta1 and Theta2, while summary() of “inla.spde2.pcmatern” is reporting Range and Stdev for the spatial effects. For me it seemed intuitive to use “inla.spde2.matern” and corresponding Theta1 and Theta2 in “inla.tmarginal…”, but that was obliviously giving wrong results. Thanks for pointing out that default parameterization is not log(sigma) in that case. Anyways, it’s clear now.

Regards,

Ivan

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Barrier model marginal variances
messages.body_plain:
The reason that the "raw" inla output only gives the internal
theta1&theta2 parameterisation is that the code handles user-defined
parameterisations, including non-stationary models, where there is no
closed form expression for the variance(s) or range(s).
inla.spde.result does it's best to produce "nominal" variances and
ranges in those cases, and for the default parameterisation that's the
actual variance and range (except for boundary effects). This is the
only automated method for accessing those, but the documentation for
inla.spde2.matern does give the full expressions for the
parameterisation.  Se also this paper for more details and
recommendations when using inla.spde2.matern():
https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19

The pcmatern priors tend to be preferable to the log-normal priors in
inla.spde2.matern(), so unless you're working with non-stationary
models, I recommend inla.spde2.pcmatern(), which provides more
user-readable results since it only supports a single, stationary,
parameterisation.

Finn

Anyone have any example about this? ¿Is more fast in comparison with the classic parameterization?

Thanks

messages.subject_clean: inlabru ipoint() for polygon samplers
messages.body_plain:
Hi R-inla,

I am a fairly new user to Bayesian statistics and INLA, and have been trying to develop a point process distribution model using inlabru.

I have survey data covering a single large site over multiple (4) years. The transects themselves have a single width and vary spatially within each year. I have been using the lgcp() function to build the model. For now I have been using the empirical bayesian approach (init.tutorial()).

Building the model separately for each year separately appears to fit the data well. Building the model using data for every year and including the year/season (using the code below) appears to fit the data for each year reasonably well, although predictions are less precise.

cmp.year <- coordinates  + IYear ~ spat(map = coordinates,
                                        group = IYear,
                                        ngroup = nyear,
                                        model = inla.spde2.matern(mesh)) + Intercept

fit.all <- lgcp(components = cmp.year,
                 data = Data.All.Years,
                 samplers = Transects_All)

As I understand from the following vignette (https://github.com/fbachl/inlabru/blob/devel/vignettes/web/2d_lgcp_spatiotemporal.Rmd), I need to construct the integration points for each year independently, and that the above code results in an aggregation of each years sampling regions.

However, running the following code does not seem to work. R is taking an exceptionally long time to process this, and when I have left this to run overnight, R has simply crashed. Transects_All is a Spatial Polygon created from line transects using gBuffer(Transects_All, width = 500)
ips <- ipoints(Transects_All, group = "IYear").

Calculating the integration points for the transects as SpatialLines using this method works very quickly, so I was wondering whether anybody else had come across a similar issue when trying to generate these integration points, and whether there was a known workaround?

Additional information:
- Over 4 years I have over 5000 individual points, in some areas, these points can be concentrated within a very small area.
- In some years the predictions from the lgcp model can have a handful of estimates with very large upper quantiles. I have therefore been plotting using the median output, which looks alot better.

Cheers,

Harri

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inlabru ipoint() for polygon samplers
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] inlabru ipoint() for polygon samplers
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Things to check:
1) Do you have a polygon survey area, or line transect data?
 For line transect data with a narrow transect width, the usual option is to specify the samplers as a SpatialLines object, making the assumption that the cross transect variability of the point intensity is approximately linear perpendicularly to the transect.
2) check that your “500” is in the same units as your mesh. (E.g. so you don’t have a mix of longlat and metres, for instance)
3) the coordinates+lYear ~ notation should give you the right thing already i think; you may be able to use debug() to step into the code that calls ipoints() internally for that model, to see what it actually does. Unfortunately getting to that part of the code may be a challenge.

Depending on the outcome of the above checks, upgrading to the latest github devel version may make a difference. The next major devel upgrade is a couple of weeks away at least.

Finn

messages.subject: Combining areal data from differential spatial resolutions
messages.subject_clean: Combining areal data from differential spatial resolutions
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am interested in combining areal data from multiple scales into one spatio-temporal model.

To be specific, suppose we have a dataset of county-level outcomes from the year 2000 onwards. Before 2000 we only have access to the national-level outcome and the population in each county. We assume that the national outcome is a population weighted mean of the county outcomes.

What I'd like to do is fit a spatio-temporal model at the county level which also uses the aggregated national data before 2000.

The last example in the Blangiardo and Cameletti book covers lowering the spatial resolution of spatial data, but I'm interested in combining data at multiple resolutions. The spatialfusion <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/spatialfusion/index.html> package and related paper is relevant in that it combines multiple forms of spatial data, but it looks like it doesn't support multiple datasets of the same type (i.e. multiple areal datasets at different resolutions.)

Should I be looking more into the inla.stack function? Or using multiple likelihoods and the copy function? Tips on where to go next would be appreciated. Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Performing a replicate study using INLA. Are all the results the same ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Performing a replicate study using INLA. Are all the results the same ?
messages.body_plain:
Apart from the slight numerical differences due to parallelisation, inla is a deterministic method for obtaining estimates of Bayesian posterior distributions. MCMC is a stochastic method for obtaining such estimates. You should expect to get different results from each MCMC run due to the inherent randomness (unless you use the same random seed each time), but inla should be expected to give the same answer each time. It’s a classic variance/bias tradeoff: MCMC has large variance but (hopefully) no bias. Inla has no variance but does have a small bias.

You need to ask yourself _why_ you would want different results from inla each time.
The suggestion of using inla.posterior.sample() just turns one step of inla into a Monte Carlo (independent samples, not MCMC) sampler, which is useful in some situations, but it’s not clear from your question what it is you’re actually indenting to achieve.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Finn and Helpdesk for your replies.
Finn  thanks for your interest, what I am trying to do is recovering parameters of a model using simulated data. As it is simulated my model doesn't have problem to recover the parameters. For reporting my results I would also like to use the Root Mean Square Error with many samples of the parameters and response variable.

Ing. Carlos Jeffer García C.

El mar., 8 oct. 2019 a las 9:55, Finn Lindgren (<finn.l...@gmail.com>) escribió:

> Apart from the slight numerical differences due to parallelisation, inla is a deterministic method for obtaining estimates of Bayesian posterior distributions. MCMC is a stochastic method for obtaining such estimates. You should expect to get different results from each MCMC run due to the inherent randomness (unless you use the same random seed each time), but inla should be expected to give the same answer each time. It’s a classic variance/bias tradeoff: MCMC has large variance but (hopefully) no bias. Inla has no variance but does have a small bias.
>
> You need to ask yourself _why_ you would want different results from inla each time.

> The suggestion of using inla.posterior.sample() just turns one step of inla into a Monte Carlo (independent samples, not MCMC) sampler, which is useful in some situations, but it’s not clear from your question what it is you’re actually indenting to achieve.
>
> Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Performing a replicate study using INLA. Are all the results the same ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Performing a replicate study using INLA. Are all the results the same ?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, inla.rmarginal only provides samples from marginal (posterior)
distributions, whereas inla.posterior.sample produces joint samples
from the entire model.
If the quantity you want to sample from only depends on a single
variable for which INLA has provided the marginal distribution, then
you could use inla.rmarginal (plus conditional data level sampling)
instead of inla.posterior.sample.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
An analogue to p-value is exceedance probability, an analogue to confidence interval is credible interval.
If you want the typical 1 star, 2 star, 3 star things, you have to computer it manually from the marginal distributions.

Credible intervals are what one gets from quantiles of the posterior, as in the code shown. Confidence intervals are defined from the sampling distribution of a point estimator, and requires other methods to compute. It is not only a matter of different interpretation.

 Confidence intervals are well defined even in Bayesian contexts, and are quite separate from credible intervals; they may be close in practice, but have completely separate definitions.

Finn

https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/8870/46ae39f2c9d8eba3fb85008c0a047b3484fd.pdf

especially this slide:

Problem is, frequentists never have to defend their methods but Bayesians do ...

messages.subject: Error "Illegal instruction" in inla.qinv()
messages.subject_clean: Error "Illegal instruction" in inla.qinv()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I tried to fit a basic logistic regression model with `inla()` on my local (Linux) computer. Everything runs fine.
However, doing the same on a Linux server I get the following error message:

```
Illegal instruction Warning in system(paste(shQuote(inla.getOption("inla.call")), "-s -m qinv", : running command ''/usr/local/lib/R/site-library/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/inla.run' -s -m qinv -r auto -S default /tmp/RtmpGnRGSy/file118690a27 /tmp/RtmpGnRGSy/file17a275729 /tmp/RtmpGnRGSy/file12c5c2884' had status 132 The INLA model could not be fitted for isPositive ~ 1 + f(timeId, model = 'linear') + f(spatialId, model = 'bym2', graph = neighb.adj, scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE, hyper = list(phi = list(prior = 'pc', param = c(phi.u, phi.alpha), initial = -3), prec = list(prior = 'pc.prec', param = c(u, alpha), initial = 5))) -- Message -- file.exists(filename) is not TRUE
```

So, the `inla.qinv()` tries to write a file via command line which fails.
I would like to understand why it fails, what is status 132? Is the file too large, or could it be a permission issue?

I also tried to find out where the error comes from in the code. Therefore I have set inla.setOption(debug = TRUE, silent = 0, working.directory = tempdir()).
The error occurs in inla() between lines 1668 and 1879: https://github.com/inbo/INLA/blob/master/R/inla.R
But I don't find where `inla.qinv()` is called.

Any help to understand or fix this problem is very welcome!

Machteld

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm hoping I could get some general advice for building INLA R package from source with old GLIBC (2.12) on a system where I do not have root permissions.

Through regular package install via:

install.packages("INLA", repos=c(getOption("repos"),
        INLA="https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/testing"), dep=TRUE)

library(INLA)

## example
fake.locations = matrix(c(0,0,5,5, 0, 5, 5, 0), nrow = 4, byrow = T)
mesh.sim = inla.mesh.2d(loc = fake.locations, max.edge=c(1, 1))

I get the common message which I've seen posted about before (for example here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/R2uLnUainWM)

My error message:

/mylibpath/rlibs/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/fmesher: /lib64/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.14' not found (required by /mylibpath/rlibs/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/fmesher)
/mylibpath/rlibs/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/fmesher: /lib64/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.14' not found (required by /mylibpath/rlibs/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/libgsl.so.23)
Error in fmesher.read(prefix, "manifold") :
  File '/tmp/RtmpCVHNmp/fmesher3f514160b593.manifold' does not exist.

I've tried the solution:

INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround()
mesh.sim = inla.mesh.2d(loc = fake.locations, max.edge=c(1, 1))

and I receive the error:

FATAL: kernel too old
Error in fmesher.read(prefix, "manifold") :
  File '/tmp/RtmpCVHNmp/fmesher3f51415d0b65.manifold' does not exist.

Is there any other available workarounds, or advice on how to build from source?

Thanks very much for any help or advice,
Dan

>

We discovered that the code ran on certain servers and not on others (even though the OSes were identical - both Ubuntu 18.04 LTS - and even though the Docker containers where the actual INLA code was run were identical).

We figured out that the origin of the problem was that the servers (KVM virtual machines) on which the containers were running had different virtual cpus configured. This resulted in different supported CPU flags being available on different servers. The old non-functioning virtual machine definition had

  <cpu mode='custom' match='exact'>
    <model fallback='allow'>Opteron_G3</model>
  </cpu>

whereas we left out the cpu definition out in the current (functioning) version.

messages.subject: Sharing variance parameters across multiple parameters
messages.subject_clean: Sharing variance parameters across multiple parameters
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a specific question that I cannot seem to answer myself. In short, I want multiple series, with different indexing, to share a variance parameter. I am aware that when the variables follow the same index, you can use the replicate command. However, I don't know what to do if they have different indexes altogether. Also, the copy trick doesn't work in this case. (I think...)

For example, take;
# library(INLA)
n      = 100
index1 = rep(1:3, n)
index2 = rep(1:3, each=n)

# Note that;
> head(index1)
[1] 1 2 3 1 2 3
> head(index2)
[1] 1 1 1 1 1 1

y      = rnorm(n, 0, 1)
myData = cbind.data.frame(y,index1,index2)

# what I would like is something along the lines of;
inla.formula = y ~ f(index1, model = "rw2") + f(index2, model = "rw2")
inla.model   = inla(formula, family = "gaussian", data = myData)

My question in this case is can ensure that f(index1, model = "rw2") and f(index2, model = "rw2") share the same variance parameter? Also, in this case the maximum of both variables is 3, but this could be different in my application.
In my model I want to group a few of the variance parameters to reduce the amount of hyper parameters to estimate. (I also have a reason why I think they should be similar.) My hope is, it will reduce computational time.

As always, many thanks and kind regards,
Alex

messages.subject_clean: Finding posterior covariance matrix for theta1, theta2, hopefully others
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am working with spatial data and I want to understand the covariance matrix related to the spatial hyperparameters: specifically, the scale parameter kappa, marginal variance of the process sigma_u^2, and also the nugget variance (which I understand to be the inverse of "The Precision of the Gaussian Observations" from mod$marginal.hyperpar.

mod and some other code is given below, based on that from Blangiardo for the swiss rainfall example:
spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha = 2)
formula <- rain ~ -1 + Intercept +  f(field, model=spde)
mod =   inla(formula,
             data=inla.stack.data(stack, spde=spde),
             family="gaussian",
             control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE),
             control.compute=list(cpo=TRUE, dic=TRUE),
             keep=FALSE, verbose=TRUE)
result = inla.spde2.result(mod, "field", spde)

I want to make the Gaussian assumption for these parameters, and I am using alpha=2 and d=2 (lat, lon). So it is more appropriate to use the theta1 and theta2 (which are log(tau) and log(kappa) respectively).

My question is this: Can we obtain:
the 2x2 posterior covariance matrix for (theta_1, theta_2)?
the 3x3 posterior covariance matrix for (log(eta), theta_1, theta_2), where eta is the nugget variance, that will be very good.
the 4x4 posterior covariance matrix for (log(sigma_u^2), log(eta), theta_1, theta_2), that will be great.

Thank you very much for your help!

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much for your quick response, this is helpful.

I do have a follow up question. I actually have used a sort of similar trick before when modelling jointly longitudinal and survival models. In that case there are two different ``y variables'' (one continuous, and one a ``count'' variable).

Going through your code, it seems like a similar ``trick'', i.e. have two y variables and subsequently make one long y vector of length 2 x N. My example is slightly different, because I only have 1 (vector) y variable, size 1 x N. To be more specific, my y variable is the price firms are willing to pay for real estate. On the right hand side I have many continuous variables, like firm debt, enterprise value, etc. I ``bucket'' the right hand-side variables into many quantiles, and subsequently want to look the effects in the extremes. I want to structure these parameters for obvious (signal extraction) reasons; This is why I need the f(x, model="rw2"). My problem is that I have many variables, and thus many variance parameters. Therefore I want to let them share one hyperparamter, hopefully reducing computational time, as I have 15K observations.

If I understand your example correctly, I would have to duplicate the y variable for every x variable that I use? This would blow up the data going into INLA to over 100K. So I am afraid this would actually hurt computational time...

Any thoughts? Many thanks again,

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I do not this that this e-mail got a reply…

> I found the estimation of  rho is significantly affected by the value of  beta1 and beta2 ，only in appropriate value the estimate works well.(eg: when set beta1=8,beta2=2,the result is very bad.) It puzzles me  cause I don‘t know how to choose appropriate value,it seems like I can only try different values blindly.I tried to find how people simulate data,all I found are real examples not simulations.

I think that this happens because the variability in the covariates is larger than the one that you include in the random effects.

> I am totally have no idea about this simple basic problem,it's very kind of you to help.There is my code,by the way,I'm worry about creating inappropriate spatial weight matrix so I use matrix in data(boston) instead.

My advice is that you choose a different simulation study with a better balance between the fixed and random effects. For example, reduce the standard deviations of x1 and x2 to 1 and 2, respectively, This will reduce the variability in the fixed part of the model and will allow you to identify the fixed effects and spatial pattern better. See attached file.

My feeling is that if you allow too much variability in the covariates this may confound with the smaller variability in the random effects, i.e., the model will not be able to tell whether the variability observed comes from the covariate or the random effect.

Best,

Virgilio

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

As a newbie to INLA, I studied the examples in book: Spatial and Spatio-temporal Bayesian Models with R-INLA, which shows univariate space-time model as well as joint modeling of multiple distributions for spatial data. But my actual use case is to deal with multivariate space-time data and I'm not sure how to order/group the data structure when modeling as a whole with INLA. Is there any example code to model multivariate space-time data with R-INLA?

First and most important, I want to make sure INLA could handle such a model, if it does, then I could go into details how to model my multivariate spatio-temporal big data.

Any input/suggestion would be appreciated!

messages.subject: (default) units for distances in inla.mesh.2d() and how to change them?
messages.subject_clean: (default) units for distances in inla.mesh.2d() and how to change them?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm new to INLA, so please excuse my question in case I'm asking something obvious. I didn't find an answer looking at literature or other posts in this discussion group, though.

The default for points to create a mesh in inla.mesh.2d() seems to be a matrix with points (possibly also in UTM). My study area spans the entire conterminous US, i.e. 10 UTM zones - so conversion to UTM isn't really a thing here.
I decided to keep it in Long/Lat and made use of the crs = argument. When I now started to try around with the mesh I was confused about the units for max.edge, cutoff etc.
Initially I thought the units would be meters or kilometers but I got meshes with extremely few nodes  & triangles (see 1. image). Initially I thought the units would be meters or kilometers.

crs1 <- CRS ("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84")
mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(Loc, max.edge=c(100, 1000), cutoff = 20, crs = crs1)

After some playing around i now think that inla.mesh.2d automatically uses the same units as the input CRS: 1° is around 111 km at 40° Latitude and converting starts to give reasonable results.

mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d (Loc, max.edge = c(100, 1000)/111, cutoff = 20/111, crs = crs1)

Clarification would still be appreciated, so that I can correctly state the parameters that I used.
And maybe there's even a way to specify the unit? changing the unit to "km" or "m" in the CRS-ojbect ("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +units=km") didn't change anything -

Best,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] (default) units for distances in inla.mesh.2d() and how to change them?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] (default) units for distances in inla.mesh.2d() and how to change them?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The mesh units are always based on the raw coordinates as they are stored in the object, i.e. in whatever units you create it. Optionally, in the creation they can be converted into a specific CRS without first converting the inputs. So with longlat as CRS the interpretation of the distance unit depends on the latitude.
For domains large enough for this to make a difference, I prefer working on spherical meshes, which allows setting max.edge in radians (degree*pi/180). inla.CRS(“sphere”) can be used to specify the needed CRS for that.

An exception to this is the inlabru package, where the intensities for log-gaussian cox processes is automatically constructed as being per km^2, if a CRS is present.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] (default) units for distances in inla.mesh.2d() and how to change them?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] (default) units for distances in inla.mesh.2d() and how to change them?
messages.body_plain:
Just note that if your domain is large (e.g. a sizable fraction of the size of a small country like Scotland or larger) I would highly recommend converting to km instead of m, to avoid numerical precision errors. This can be done on an existing mesh via inla.spTransform, using a CRS with +units=km, if I recall the syntax correctly. This works if the original CRS has units in metres, like UTM.

Finn

> On 23 Oct 2019, at 16:14, Vincent von Dosky <vincent...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿

> Hi Finn,
>
> Thank you, that all makes sense now.
>
> My issue arose, because I imported Lat/Long directly from the table in which all other measures for those points are stored.
> Just using the shapefile with my sampling locations instead fixed it right away, as it has the unit in it's PROJ.4 format stored. Now I can set max.edge values in meters, which is more tangible.
>
> I will definitely look at inla.CRS("sphere"). Thanks for pointing that out!
>
> Best,
> Vincent
>
> On Wednesday, October 23, 2019 at 2:34:47 PM UTC+2, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > Hi,shapefile
> > The mesh units are always based on the raw coordinates as they are stored in the object, i.e. in whatever units you create it. Optionally, in the creation they can be converted into a specific CRS without first converting the inputs. So with longlat as CRS the interpretation of the distance unit depends on the latitude.
> > For domains large enough for this to make a difference, I prefer working on spherical meshes, which allows setting max.edge in radians (degree*pi/180). inla.CRS(“sphere”) can be used to specify the needed CRS for that.
> >
> > An exception to this is the inlabru package, where the intensities for log-gaussian cox processes is automatically constructed as being per km^2, if a CRS is present.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > > On 23 Oct 2019, at 12:08, Vincent von Dosky <vincent...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > I decided to keep it in Long/Lat and made use of the crs = argument. When I now started to try around with the mesh I was confused about the units for max.edge, cutoff etc.

messages.body_plain:
I'm trying a variation of the example : Swiss rainfall data in section 6.10 of the book spatial and spatio-temporal data modeling with R-INLA,
where I wanted to include the covariate: elevation to do the prediction, due to the high number of prediction locations, I'm following the trick to project the latent field onto prediction grid locations.
As in this code:
A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=Swiss.mesh, loc=est.coord)
A.val <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=Swiss.mesh) #, loc=val.coord
stack.val <- inla.stack(data = list(rain=NA),
                        A = list(A.val,1),
                        effects = list(c(s.index, list(Intercept=1)), list(Elevation=val.elevation)),
                        tag="val")

Because the A.val projection matrix has a smaller size, I got the error "Row count mismatch for A" in the stack.val. Is it possible to do the prediction with that covariate while using the trick here? I'm not sure how to assemble the inla.stack() if it could do.
I'm also guessing, this trick might only available for the latent field?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,  I am a beginner user to R & Rinla and I'm running into an error I'm hoping someone can help with.  I am receiving this error:

Error in data.frame(NAME = names, y = y, E = E, x1 = x1, x2 = x2) :
  object 'E' not found
In addition: Warning message:
readShapePoly is deprecated; use rgdal::readOGR or sf::st_read

The code I am using is based off of Chapter 6.1 code found from this textbook & code:
Text Book:
https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/home
Code from Textbook:
http://www.statistica.it/marta/stbook/Chapter6.R

Here is the code I'm using the error comes in at line 47:

### R code for Chapter 6
### Last update: 18/08/2014

##################################################
### Set working directory and load packages
###################################################
remove(list=ls())
my.dir <- paste(getwd(),"/",sep="")

require(INLA)
inla.setOption(scale.model.default=FALSE)

require(gstat)
require(geoR)
require(fields)
require(maptools)
require(lattice)
require(spdep)

###################################################
### Code for Section 6.1.2
###################################################
# You neeed a folder called "London Suicides" inside your working directory (my.dir)
# with the data downloaded from
# https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/datasets

library(maptools)
library(spdep)

data <- read.csv(paste(my.dir,"Load_3/Block_Group_Cin.csv",sep=""))
#load(paste(my.dir,"Load_2/BlockGroupCin_Real.csv",sep=""))
london.gen <- readShapePoly(paste(my.dir,"Load_3/Cincinnati_Block_Group.shp",sep=""))

temp <- poly2nb(london.gen)
nb2INLA("LDN.graph", temp)
LDN.adj <- paste(getwd(),"/LDN.graph",sep="")

H <- inla.read.graph(filename="LDN.graph")
image(inla.graph2matrix(H),xlab="",ylab="")

formula <- y ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym",graph=LDN.adj, scale.model=TRUE,
                     hyper=list(prec.unstruct=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.001)), prec.spatial=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.001))))

names <- sort(london.gen$NAME)
data.suicides <- data.frame(NAME=names, y=y, E=E, x1=x1, x2=x2)
Nareas <- length(data.suicides[,1])

# The order of the areas needs to be the same between the data and the spatial polygon object obtained importing the shapefile, so we re-order the data
data.boroughs <- attr(london.gen, "data")
order <- match(data.boroughs$NAME,data.suicides$NAME)
data.suicides <- data.suicides[order,]
data.suicides$ID <- seq(1,Nareas)
# Include in the london.gen dataframe the ID variable  1:32 (because SP_Id is 0:31)
attr(london.gen, "data") <- merge(data.boroughs,data.suicides,by="NAME")

mod.suicides <- inla(formula,family="poisson",
                     data=data.suicides,E=E,
                     control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

round(mod.suicides$summary.fixed,3)
round(head(mod.suicides$summary.random$ID),3) #partial output

exp.b0.mean <- inla.emarginal(exp,mod.suicides$marginals.fixed[[1]])
exp.b0.mean
exp.b0.95CI <- inla.qmarginal(c(0.025,0.975), inla.tmarginal(exp,mod.suicides$marginals.fixed[[1]]))
exp.b0.95CI

# *** Code for Figure 6.6 left
csi <- mod.suicides$marginals.random$ID[1:Nareas]
zeta <- lapply(csi,function(x) inla.emarginal(exp,x))
# Define the cutoff for zeta
zeta.cutoff <- c(0.6, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.8)
# Transform zeta in categorical variable
cat.zeta <- cut(unlist(zeta),breaks=zeta.cutoff,include.lowest=TRUE)
# Create a dataframe with all the information needed for the map
maps.cat.zeta <- data.frame(ID=data.suicides$ID, cat.zeta=cat.zeta)
# Add the categorized zeta to the spatial polygon
data.boroughs <- attr(london.gen, "data")
attr(london.gen, "data") <- merge(data.boroughs, maps.cat.zeta, by="ID")

trellis.par.set(axis.line=list(col=NA))
spplot(obj=london.gen, zcol= "cat.zeta", col.regions=gray(seq(0.9,0.1,length=4)), asp=1)
# ***

# *** Code for Figure 6.6 right
a <- 0
prob.csi <- lapply(csi, function(x) {1 - inla.pmarginal(a, x)})
prob.csi.cutoff <- c(0,0.2,0.8,1)
cat.prob.csi <- cut(unlist(prob.csi),breaks=prob.csi.cutoff, include.lowest=TRUE)
maps.cat.prob.csi <- data.frame(ID=data.suicides$ID, cat.prob.csi=cat.prob.csi)
data.boroughs <- attr(london.gen, "data")
attr(london.gen, "data") <- merge(data.boroughs, maps.cat.prob.csi, by="ID")

spplot(obj=london.gen, zcol= "cat.prob.csi", col.regions=gray(seq(0.9,0.1,length=3)))
# ***

mat.marg <- matrix(NA, nrow=Nareas, ncol=100000)
m <- mod.suicides$marginals.random$ID
for (i in 1:Nareas){
  # Remember that the first Nareas values of the random effects
  # are u+v, while u values are stored in the Nareas+1 to 2*Nareas elements.
  u <- m[[Nareas+i]]

  mat.marg[i,] <- inla.rmarginal(100000, u)
}
var.u <- apply(mat.marg, 2, var)

var.v <- inla.rmarginal(100000,inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1/x,
                                              mod.suicides$marginals.hyper$"Precision for ID (iid component)"))
perc.var.u <- mean(var.u/(var.u+var.v))
perc.var.u

marg.hyper <- inla.hyperpar.sample(100000,mod.suicides)
perc.var.u1 <- mean(marg.hyper[,1] / (marg.hyper[,1]+marg.hyper[,2]))
perc.var.u1

###################################################
### Code for Section 6.2 (run the code for Section 6.1.2 first)
###################################################
formula.eco.reg <- y ~ 1 + x1 + x2 + f(ID,model="bym", graph=LDN.adj)

mod.eco.reg <- inla(formula.eco.reg,family="poisson",
                    data=data.suicides,E=E,
                    control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

mod.eco.reg$dic$dic

# *** Code for Figure 6.7 left
csi.eco.reg <- mod.eco.reg$marginals.random$ID[1:Nareas]
zeta.eco.reg <- lapply(csi.eco.reg,function(x) inla.emarginal(exp,x))
# Define the cutoff for zeta
zeta.cutoff <- c(0.6, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.8)
# Transform zeta in categorical variable
cat.zeta.eco.reg <- cut(unlist(zeta.eco.reg),breaks=zeta.cutoff,include.lowest=TRUE)
# Create a dataframe with all the information needed for the map
maps.cat.zeta.eco.reg <- data.frame(ID=data.suicides$ID, cat.zeta.eco.reg=cat.zeta.eco.reg)
# Add the categorized zeta to the spatial polygon dataframe object london.gen
data.boroughs <- attr(london.gen, "data")

spplot(obj=london.gen, zcol= "cat.zeta.eco.reg", col.regions=gray(seq(0.9,0.1,length=4)))
# ***

messages.subject: Argument "control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE)" markedly slows computation
messages.subject_clean: Argument "control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE)" markedly slows computation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm performing spatial regression so interested in extracting model residuals, in particular to look at residual autocorrelation. I initially forgot the argument "control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE)," and the model in question took about 2 hours to run. Adding this in is really slowing things down-- we're at 23 hours with no results.

Do you have any suggestions of how to speed this up? Or should I just use the linear predictor and random effects? My code is below; "dengue" is a data frame, each row is a district-month (district=ubigeo), and outcome is an indicator variable for whether that district-month experienced a dengue outbreak. I'm working on a remote server (Linux) and have been asked to keep my work to 4 cores (hence the num.threads argument).

Thank you,
Julianne

---------------------------------------------------------------------
formula <- outbreak_bin ~ 1 + nino.binary3.4  + as.factor(region.natural) + bs(dengue$time, knots = (19*4-1)) + f(ubigeo.struct,model="besag",
graph="ENSO.graph") + f(ubigeo.unstruct,model="iid")

N34 <- inla(formula, family="binomial", data=dengue, Ntrials=1, verbose=FALSE, num.threads = inla.getOption("num.threads"), control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

Sorry for posting twice in one day-- this is regarding a different project, I think the issue with the first one is resolved (running now).

I'm getting the following error message when running the code attached below:

Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.

I'm running with verbose=TRUE, but there is no further output. cattle_data is a spatial points data frame, num.cattle is a count/integer, as is clustermembers.cattle. My goal here is continuous mapping.

Any guidance would be appreciated.

Julianne

-------------------------------
coords<-cattle_data@coords #6,599 coordinates
loc = as.matrix(coords)
loc.mesh = loc
mesh = inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain = loc.mesh,
                    max.edge = c(0.3,0.6),
                    offset = c(1, 1))
A<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=coords)
spde_RE<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha=2)
iset <- inla.spde.make.index('i', n.spde=spde_RE$n.spde)#no ST interaction

stk.dat.c<-inla.stack(
  data=list(resp=cattle_data@data$num.cattle),
  A=list(A,1),
  effects=list(iset,
  data.frame(intercept = rep(1, nrow(cattle_data@data)),
             urban=cattle_data@data$urban)),
  tag='est')

f.spde.urb <- resp ~ 0 + intercept + urban + f(i, model=spde_RE)
res.spde.c.urb<-inla (f.spde.urb, data=inla.stack.data(stk.dat.c), family="zeroinflatedpoisson1", offset=log(cattle_data@data$clustermembers.cattle), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.dat.c)),
                      num.threads = inla.getOption("num.threads"), control.compute=list(config = TRUE), verbose=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
you're out of memory. try with

control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb', strategy = 'adaptive')

you're out of memory. try with

control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb', strategy = 'adaptive')

On Wed, 2019-10-30 at 11:00 -0700, Julianne Meisner wrote:
> Thanks, I upgraded and it worked for the m

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Argument "control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE)" markedly slows computation
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Argument "control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE)" markedly slows computation
messages.body_plain:
in general, fewer number of threads will use less memory, so you may
get away with

control.inla = list(strategy = 'adaptive')

and setting

inla(...., num.threads=2)

messages.body_plain:
I'm studying the github book: Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA <http://www.r-inla.org/spde-book>
https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-manipula.html

In the section of coregionalization, it specified prior distribution for the lambda's(coef's of the copied spatial effects)
hyper <- list(theta = list(prior = 'normal', param = c(0, 10)))
then used here in the modeling via control family:
result <- inla(form, rep('gaussian', 3),
  data = inla.stack.data(stack),
  control.family = list(hyper.eps, hyper.eps, hyper.eps),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack)),
  control.mode = list(theta = theta.ini, restart = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb'))
If I understand it correctly, the control.mode is specifying the initial value of the hyper-parameters, whilecontrol.family specifies the distribution of the hyper-parameters? (The documents of control.mode and control.family doesn't really help much)
I wonder why the control.family only specify the COEF's prior distribution for the model, other hyper-parameters are set already by default?

messages.body_plain:
control.mode shouldn't really be used (but we need it to do something
automatic), and I wouldn't not worry to much about this. initial
values can always be defined where its used, using 'initial'.

'Give me a list of which priors that is used', a relevant issue.
sometime ago, I added this function which does that (that was pretty
intricate), but you'll see an example below, from the demo(Bym)
example, just to have a non-trivial one.

hope this helps.
H

> data(Germany)
> g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
> source(system.file("demodata/Bym-map.R", package="INLA"))
Read 3921 items
> summary(Germany)
> Germany = cbind(Germany,region.struct=Germany$region)
> # standard BYM model
> formula1 = Y ~ f(region.struct,model="besag",graph=g) +
+                f(region,model="iid")

> result1  =  inla(formula1,family="poisson",data=Germany,E=E)

> inla.priors.used(result1)
section=[family]
	tag=[INLA.Data1] component=[poisson]
section=[fixed]
	tag=[(Intercept)] component=[(Intercept)]
		beta:
			parameter=[(Intercept)]
			prior=[normal]
			param=[0, 0]
section=[random]
	tag=[region.struct] component=[region.struct]
		theta1:
			parameter=[log precision]
			prior=[loggamma]
			param=[1e+00, 5e-05]
		group.theta1:
			parameter=[logit correlation]
			prior=[normal]
			param=[0.0, 0.2]
	tag=[region] component=[region]
		theta1:
			parameter=[log precision]
			prior=[loggamma]
			param=[1e+00, 5e-05]
		group.theta1:
			parameter=[logit correlation]
			prior=[normal]

	inla.prior.used(result)

	plot(result, plot.prior=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA users,

I am fitting a space-time log Gaussian Cox process model with covariates and am coming unstuck when trying to generate spatial predictions. I would like to generate a lot of predictions from this model, somewhere in the region of 24 different spatial predictions of the entire mesh.

Following the INLA tutorials I have tried to generate spatial predictions while fitting the model. I have appended a dataframe of covariate values from which I want to generate predictions and have included a column of NAs for the Y/ Frequency column. I have also specified link = 1 and compute = TRUE in the `control.predictor` argument.

The model runs fine when there is no prediction data, but when I include the NAs I get the following error:

file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: 0bed76828f01  date: Tue Sep 03 11:21:49 2019 +0300
Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 876, Thread: 0
Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...

Can anyone shed light on why I might be getting this error?

Following this post: http://www.r-inla.org/events/problemswithopenblas I have tried `inla.setOption(mkl = TRUE) but this does not resolve the issue.

Alternatively, given that I am planning on generating so many predicted surfaces should I try an alternative method to generate predictions? For example by sampling from the posterior instead?

Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Many thanks,

James

Here is my model set up. I am working on a Windows server with 44 cores and 512GB memory.

A.st <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = smesh,
                         loc = smesh$loc[agg.dat$area, ],
                         group = agg.dat$season,
                         n.group = k,
                         mesh.group = tmesh)

idx <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 's',
                            n.spde = barrier.model$f$n,
                            n.group = k)

stk <- inla.stack(data = list(y = agg.dat$Freq,
                              exposure = agg.dat$exp_adj),
                  A = list(A.st, 1),
                  effects = list(idx,
                                 list(b0 = rep(1, nrow(agg.dat)),
                                      x_bar = agg.dat$x_bar,
                                      x_bar_c_s = agg.dat$x_bar_c_s,
                                      x_bar_c_s_m = agg.dat$x_bar_c_s_m,
                                      x_res_smy = agg.dat$x_res_smy)))

pcrho <- list(theta = list(prior = 'pccor1', param = c(.7, .7)))

f_1 <- y ~ -1 + b0 + x_bar + x_bar_c_s + x_bar_c_s_m + x_res_smy +
  f(s,
    model = barrier.model,
    group = s.group,
    replicate = s.repl,
    control.group = list(model = 'ar1',
                         hyper = pcrho))

m_1 <- inla(f_1,
            family = 'poisson',
            data = inla.stack.data(stk),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk),
                                     link = 1,
                                     compute = TRUE),
            E = agg.dat$exp_adj,
            control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian",
                                int.strategy = "eb"),
            control.compute = list(openmp.strategy = "huge",
                                   config = TRUE,
                                   dic = T,
                                   waic = T),
                        control.mode = list(theta = c(1.323, 7.089, 0.643), restart = T),
            verbose = T,
            num.threads = 16) # switch on when trialling
